The Situational Awareness situation.

It is now being reported that the AI hedge fund has exited its entire public equity portfolio this month.

But, what does this really mean?

As of July 1st, the Net Asset Value (NAV) of the fund is now being reported to have been ~$45 billion.

First, let's put this into perspective.

NAV = (Assets − Liabilities). This is the fund's equity capital, also known as the investors' money after accounting for borrowings.

This is NOT the same as the size of the fund's positions, particularly because the fund has been known for utilizing extreme amounts of leverage. For example:

1. At 2x leverage, a $45 billion NAV supports ~$90 billion of gross market exposure
2. At 3x leverage, that rises to ~$135 billion
3. At 4x leverage, that rises to ~ $180 billion

This means that exiting its "public equity book" does not necessarily imply $45 billion of stock changed hands. It was likely much more.

Depending on the fund's leverage and portfolio construction, the gross amount of securities unwound could have been well in excess of $100 billion.

When considering these facts, the market has actually held up exceptionally well.

There has never been an era of investing like the AI era.

Volatility is the new normal.

My thoughts on the Fed that told us nothing and how the bond market responded. 

Rates unchanged yesterday, exactly as I told you. 

That was the easy part. What came with it was nothing. No forward guidance, not one sentence about September. The statement barely moved except for the dissent list.

3 dissents. Logan, Hammack, Kashkari, all for 25 bps. FinX called it a hawkish tell. It isn’t. Warsh wants the argument in the open, where prior chairs got unanimity that was mostly theater. So 3 dissents under him means less, not more, and those 3 have been the hawkish end of the table all along.

The market moved my way. September hike odds fell to 60% from 80%. Fewer people believe a hike is coming, not more, and that number still has room to fall.

Now the part everyone should be focusing on.

The most important market yesterday was Treasuries. The 30-year rose 12.1 bps to 5.213%, highest since 2007. Real yields rose with it, so the actual cost of capital got worse. 10s2s steepened. That is a bond market pricing a Fed behind the curve, and pricing it aggressively.

The fear is not really about oil. What’s spooking the long end is AI capex. Chips and memory. Power. Copper, silver and gold all higher the same day. One commodity rising is a story about that commodity. All of them rising at once is capital being fire hosed into every physical corner of the economy.

I’ll say the thing I always say, because I believe it and because it limits how far I’ll push this. Sustained inflation is a monetary phenomenon. Oil doubling is a relative price change. But when hundreds of billions chase a fixed stock of transformers, turbines, HBM capacity and electricians on four-year lead times, the money is real and the supply is finite, and the bond market has decided that’s close enough. Whether it’s textbook correct matters less than the 30-year sitting at 5.21% and still climbing.

Which gives you the ugliest setup I’ve seen in a while, because stocks and bonds want opposite things.

Stocks want a cut, or a clear one-and-done hike so the pain has an end date. Bonds want a hike badly, because that’s the only way this Fed shows resolve on inflation. Bonds aren’t asking nicely. They’re selling until they get an answer.

The best outcome for both is the Fed telegraphing 25 bps for September. Calms the long end, doesn’t signal a cycle. I don’t think they deliver it, same as I didn’t think they’d hike.

Until they do, you’re long a tape where the bond market votes against you every day.

I get the concern but I'd measure or phrase it a bit differently.

-It's less of an attack, imo, and more-so the existing system adopting to the latest tech to keep extending itself. And notably, people who *use* the existing system built stablecoins, not the system itself (e.g. stablecoins were built on the margins, and only when they grew large did Uncle Sam realize it could benefit them). This is inevitably going to last a long time, imo. Those that consider it an attack should buckle in.

-Taxes are a friction, which is why I support tax exemptions on modest btc spending amounts (as a realistic start) rather than the focus on crypto securities that recent legislation emphasizes. But it's not surprising that this part keeps getting dropped, and that has to be expected. They're not going to make it easy.

-People want their near-term capital to be relatively stable. And they often want what they are paid in to match their liabilities (what they owe others). Those aspects contribute to why, organically, stablecoins are quite desired globally (less-so in the US, where we have countless USD payment options).

-Stablecoins can be frozen/confiscated, unlike bitcoin. But for people who perceive themselves as low risk of being targeted that way and with small/medium amounts, millions of people simply don't run into that freezing/confiscation problem and so they enjoy those other aspects of stablecoins for working capital and payments. Those that need or want the more permissionless aspect are more likely to be early bitcoin adopters for MoE.

-Imo, the stepping stone to keep bitcoin on the SoV-MoE-UoA pathway is to make sure it's increasingly *exchangeable*. In other words, a key reason why a gold coin is valuable is because I can carry it with me globally, and pretty easily find a buyer for it almost anywhere at a decent market price. I can't easily buy goods or services with it directly (because it's not what businesses use as their working capital or what they have liabilities denominated in), but I can convert it readily to whatever the local money is in most places. That global exchange feature is something I can't do with most other SoVs like stocks. Bitcoin scores decently in that regard but needs to keep getting better. That intermediate step is a key stepping stone to further improve. Expecting massive volumes of btc last-mile payments any time soon is going to lead to disappointment, imo, even though it's important to build the infrastructure for it (and plan company burn rates for the long haul, rather than be shocked when volumes don't explode a couple years in). But expecting to be able to exchange bitcoin for liquid value in most places you go like gold without much friction is a more intermediate-term realistic expectation to keep working toward, with high-volume MoE further out.

-People want their near-term capital to be relatively stable. And they often want what they are paid in to match their liabilities (what they owe others). -Stablecoins can be frozen/confiscated, unlike bitcoin. That global exchange feature is something I can't do with most other SoVs like stocks. Bitcoin scores decently in that regard but needs to keep getting better. That intermediate step is a key stepping stone to further improve. Expecting massive volumes of btc last-mile payments any time soon is going to lead to disappointment, imo, even though it's important to build the infrastructure for it (and plan company burn rates for the long haul, rather than be shocked when volumes don't explode a couple years in). But expecting to be able to exchange bitcoin for liquid value in most places you go like gold without much friction is a more intermediate-term realistic expectation to keep working toward, with high-volume MoE further out.
